identity.title: Identification of mitophagy inducers for Alzheimer's disease via high-throughput endogenous ATP5B tagging system.

content.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Mitophagy, the selective clearance of defective mitochondria via the autophagy-lysosome pathway, is essential for maintaining mitochondrial health and cellular homeostasis. Dysregulation of mitophagy is strongly implicated in aging-related pathologies, including neurodegenerative diseases (Alzheimer's, Parkinson's), cancer, and metabolic disorders, highlighting the significance of elucidating its regulatory mechanisms. While existing methods using exogenous reporters enable genome-wide and high-throughput screening for mitophagy regulators, they constrain discoveries to specific pathways and introduce artifacts through ectopic expression. OBJECTIVES: To overcome these limitations, we developed an effective and rapid platform for identifying mitophagy modulators by targeting endogenous proteins. METHODS: Using CRISPR-Cas9 technology, we engineered HeLa cells expressing small molecular tags (GFP or NanoLuc) fused to the C-terminal of ATP5B, a mitochondrial inner membrane protein. Genome-wide screening for mitophagy regulatory genes were performed using a genome-wide CRISPR library coupled with flow cytometry. Additionally, an FDA-approved kinase inhibitor library was used to screen for mitophagy inducers. To evaluate the efficacy of a screened drug in Alzheimer's disease, cognitive behavior, pathological features and mitophagy events in 3 x Tg-AD mice with or without treatment were examined using the Morris water maze assay, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM). RESULTS: These ATP5B-tagging cells provided a robust readout of mitophagy and enabled high-throughput genetic or pharmacological screening. With this platform, we identified several promising genes that regulate mitophagy and are significantly associated with Alzheimer's disease. Moreover, the FDA-approved drug Flupentixol emerged as a novel mitophagy inducer that acts by promoting adenosine monophosphate-activated protein kinase (AMPK) localization to mitochondria and exhibited strong therapeutic potential in a model of Alzheimer's disease. CONCLUSION: This study establishes a novel system for identifying mitophagy modulators, with the potential to accelerate the discovery of therapeutic strategies for Alzheimer's disease.
